newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia crop low, but traders don't see big imports.
newsitem.headline: Russia crop low, but traders don't see big imports.

text.p: Russia's grain harvest was officially reported Tuesday just slightly better than last year's, which was the worst in three decades.
But grain traders in Moscow said farmers understated their output and said they doubted whether big purchases would be made from the West.
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun told a news conference that the 1996 crop was only five million metric tons above 1995's 63.4 million tons.
He said Russia would import 4.0 million to 5.0 million tons, including 2.5 to 3.0 million of high-quality wheat, in 1997.
But traders said exporting countries such as the United States, Canada and Australia should not hold their breath.
"Official data is not always realistic," said Arkady Zlochevsky, director of the prominent OGO commodities trader.
"We calculate that up to 10 percent of the harvest was hidden, making the real net figure up to 75 million tons."
He said farmers -- required to sell large parts of their grain at state prices in part to pay back credits received earlier in the season -- were simply hiding some of their production.

"We usually buy grain in Canada and Kazakhstan for blending," said a senior trader in Moscow, adding that the Central Asian republic had a good crop. "This year, I don't know if we will buy from Canada, but from Kazakhstan, definitely."
Other traders said Russia might be able to meet most of its needs with grain from non-Western suppliers and would turn to neighbouring Kazakhstan to supply some.
Khlystun said Russia's Far East and Arctic north, the regions most likely to need grain, would select private companies to import grain.
But traders said Russia's well-publicised cash crunch and tendency in recent years to announce imports but never actually carry them out had left them wary.
"I think half of the tenders announced will not happen," said a second Moscow-based trader. "There is no deficit of grain. It is just a question of different prices in different regions."

Andrei Sizov, director of the independent agricultural consultant firm SovEcon Ltd. in Moscow, said 25 percent of Russia's bread wheat crop needed to be blended with higher-quality wheat to be used for bread-making.
Only 35 percent of the total crop could be used on its own for bread, while the rest would wind up as animal feed.
But traders still said there could be enough to meet demand.
"Russia needs about 14 million tons of food-quality wheat," said the first trader, referring to annual domestic demand. "How can we not find close to that in this harvest?"
Zlochevsky said Russian imports were motivated not so much by supply and demand principles as by price.
"Exports and imports in Russia do not depend on the actual harvest as much as they do on (world) grain prices," he said.
Traders said Russia's farmers, wary about not getting paid and reluctant to sell at low state prices, were as much a factor as bad weather in the surprisingly low figure.
"This is grain which will go onto the market for cash," Zlochevsky said, referring to unreported stocks. "No documents, no taxes. Traders, almost anyone, could buy it."
